previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of living donor liver transplant for primary sclerosing cholangitis presented with sudden-onset right upper quadrant abdominal pain and elevated liver enzymes. Initial imaging showed patent hepatic vasculature but no clear cause. A transjugular liver biopsy revealed mild acute cellular rejection, prompting treatment with high-dose steroids, increased immunosuppression, and valganciclovir. Despite therapy, liver enzymes continued to rise, leading to a second biopsy that showed resolution of rejection but mild steatosis. The transaminitis was attributed to medication effects, particularly Seroquel and temazepam, both of which were discontinued. Steroid-induced mood symptoms were managed with Ativan and Seroquel, but the latter was stopped due to liver concerns. The patient improved clinically, with pain control and stabilization of labs. She was discharged on a tapering steroid regimen, adjusted immunosuppression, insulin for steroid-induced hyperglycemia, and instructions to restart clopidogrel. Follow-up was arranged for lab monitoring and outpatient evaluation.

ACUTE ISSUES
=============
#PSC c/b Cirrhosis s/p LDLT ___ 
#RUQ Pain, Fever
#Abnormal LFTs
The patient presented at the advice of her outpatient 
hepatologist when she experienced RUQ pain, body aches, chills 
and a fever to 102. In the ED she was found to have an 
ALT-predominant transaminitis (ALT 280 from baseline ___, AST 
170 from ___, an elevated AP (181 from ___, and a direct 
hyperbilirubinemia (Tbili 3.7 from 1.0, Dbili 2.8). There was 
initial concern for infection versus acute transplant rejection, 
and the patient was started empirically on vancomycin, cefepime 
and metronidazole while continuing her home immunosuppressive 
medications (cyclosporine, mycophenolate). Within 12 hours or so 
the patient was feeling significantly better, and her LFTs began 
to downtrend. Her infectious workup was thus far negative (blood 
cultures pending, UA bland, CXR normal, abdominal US without 
ascites or CBD dilation, EBV viral load pending), and given her 
rapid clinical improvement, antibiotics were discontinued at 36 
hours and it was decided that percutaneous liver biopsy to 
assess for allograft rejection was unnecessary. She was watched 
for another 24 hours off of antibiotics and continued to feel 
well, with LFTs normalizing to her baseline when she was 
discharged from the hospital. Given the rapid onset and 
resolution of this clinical picture, this may have been a 
transient biliary obstruction by a stone that passed 
spontaneously. She will be discharged with close liver 
transplant and PCP follow up.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to the hospital because at home you were 
having fevers and were found to have abnormal liver function 
tests. 

WHAT HAPPENED WHILE YOU WERE IN THE HOSPITAL?
- You were treated with antibiotics 
- We were initially concerned that you might be having another 
episode of liver transplant rejection as you did in ___, but your liver test improved on their own almost as soon 
as you got to the hospital, so we did not need to do a biopsy
- It is still not entirely clear what caused your symptoms and 
lab abnormalities, but we think you may have had a temporary 
bile duct blockage by a gall stone or sludge that resolved 
(passed into the intestine) on its own
- Even once we stopped the antibiotics, you continued to feel 
well and your lab values kept improving, so you were ready to 
leave the hospital 

WHAT DO YOU NEED TO DO WHEN YOU LEAVE THE HOSPITAL?
- Take all of your medications as prescribed (listed below)
- Keep your follow up appointments with your doctors
- Weigh yourself every morning, before you eat or take your 
medications. Call your doctor if your weight changes by more 
than 3 pounds
- Please stick to a low salt diet and monitor your fluid intake
- Seek medical attention if you have new or concerning symptoms 
or you develop fevers, chills, or abdominal pain

It was a pleasure participating in your care. We wish you the 
best!
